title: Oxidation-induced ultrafast spin-to-orbital conversion at heavy-metal interfaces
authors: Xiaoxue Zeng, Tianyi Zhang, Yaokai Niu, Qiye Wen, Zhiyong Zhong, Zhi-Min Liao, Peng Yan, Xiufeng Han, Lichuan Jin
abstract: Oxidation engineering provides a route to control orbital degrees of freedom, yet its role in spin-to-orbital conversion remains largely unexplored. Here, we report an efficient spin-to-orbital conversion mechanism driven by interfacial oxidation at heavy-metal interfaces. In W/Co/SiO2 heterostructures, terahertz emission exhibits a time delay that scales linearly with the W thickness, identifying orbital-current transport as the dominant origin. The emission amplitude is approximately three times larger than that of Co/Pt bilayers, indicating highly efficient conversion from spin to orbital angular momentum. Systematic variation of Co thickness, stoichiometry, and interface configuration reveals that the effect originates from oxidation of the W layer at the W/Co interface, which modulates the interfacial orbital texture. We further show that this mechanism is generic across different heavy metals and scales with their spin-orbit coupling strength. These results establish oxidation as an effective handle to engineer spin-to-orbital conversion and provide a general route toward orbitronic terahertz emitters.
summary: This work demonstrates that interfacial oxidation provides a powerful handle to engineer efficient conversion from spin angular momentum to orbital angular momentum in heavy-metal heterostructures. By measuring ultrafast THz emission, the authors prove this effect is maximized at oxidized interfaces, opening a general route for designing high-performance orbitronic terahertz emitters.
main_problem: The study aims to understand how interfacial oxidation can be engineered to control and enhance spin-to-orbital conversion in heavy-metal/ferromagnetic heterostructures for applications in orbitronic terahertz emitters.
main_result: Interfacial oxidation at the W/Co interface drives a highly efficient spin-to-orbital conversion, evidenced by THz emission amplitudes significantly larger than conventional bilayers. This mechanism is shown to be generic across different heavy metals and scales with their spin-orbit coupling strength.
method: The research employs time-resolved Terahertz (THz) emission spectroscopy on engineered thin-film heterostructures, complemented by structural characterization using STEM/EELS and XPS.
model_or_system: The physical system consists of multilayered metal/oxide heterostructures, primarily W/Co/SiO2. The mechanism relies on the electronic structure modification (orbital texture) induced by oxygen incorporation at the interfaces between heavy metals and ferromagnets.
key_observables: THz emission amplitude enhancement ($\sim 3	imes$ over Co/Pt), linear time delay scaling with W thickness, and chemical states confirmed via XPS.
important_parameters: Heavy metal type (e.g., Pt, Ta vs Ti, Cu), layer thicknesses ($t_W$, $t_{Co}$), and the degree of interfacial oxidation.
main_assumptions: The observed THz enhancement is directly attributable to orbital-current transport originating from the oxidized interface, which acts as a trigger for spin-to-orbital conversion.
figures_summary: Figures compare THz signals across various heterostructures and show the linear dependence of the time delay on W thickness. Structural characterization confirms interfacial intermixing and oxidation states in the critical W/Co/SiO2 structure.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by noting the unexplored role of oxidation in spin-to-orbital conversion, presents THz measurements showing enhancement in W/Co/SiO2, systematically varies layer parameters to pinpoint the oxidation mechanism, and concludes with a general framework for orbitronic emitter design.
why_interesting: While not directly related to quantum information protocols, the study involves ultrafast dynamics, spin-orbit coupling effects, and engineered electronic states, which are foundational concepts in condensed matter physics relevant to advanced quantum devices.
